3.text: disease is said to proceed from a very small insect that burrows through the

4.text: skin, probably a species of tick. Dr. Slunin mentions having seen it, though

5.text: he does not give the name of the species. It develops in mid-winter, and

6.text: the reindeer die of cold and exhaustion. This disease is also catching; and

7.text: a herd, once infected, will generally be exterminated. Sometimes the disease

8.text: will last for several years, disappear for a while, and then break out with

9.text: renewed vigor. “When it assumes a violent form, the Chukchee herdsmen

10.text: often leave the whole herd, house and everything in it, even stripping them-

11.text: selves to the last fur shirt, as a sacrifice to the spirit of the disease. Some-

12.text: times they kill all their animals, and pile them together around the tent.

13.text: According to data contained in the archives of Nishne-Kolymsk, in the spring

14.text: of 1872 a Chukchee reindeer-breeder, Tɪñeiˊmɪt, brought his whole herd, stricken

15.text: with scabies and about three thousand head strong, to that town to be

16.text: slaughtered. The inhabitants of all the neighboring villages flocked together,

17.text: and all the slaughtering was done in three days. The scabies infected the

18.text: dogs and the people, who had touched and eaten the diseased meat; but the

19.text: results were not so fatal as with the reindeer. Dr. Slunin also mentions that

20.text: scabies may be conveyed to men. Other diseases — such as muzzle-swelling,

21.text: abscesses on the sides, etc. — are of no great importance. The Chukchee

22.text: do not undertake to cure any of them, but slaughter the affected animal, and

23.text: consume it as readily as they would a healthy one. Occasionally they tie up,

24.text: a fawn’s broken leg in thin boards, or they cut open the swollen penis of a buck

25.text: that is too much affected by the rut, and sometimes they even bore with a

26.text: knife an extra outlet for the urine.

27.text: A number of beasts of prey are dangerous to the herds. The wolverine

28.text: and the black bear will occasionally kill a stray reindeer. The polar wolf is

29.text: much more dangerous, since, in the localities where the Chukchee herds are

30.text: numerous, it follows them wherever they wander, and generally lives on them.

31.text: The natives assert that there are two varieties of polar wolf. One is smaller

32.text: and swifter than the other; it hunts the wild reindeer, and never approaches

33.text: the herds, since it dreads the smell of man. The other variety is of larger

34.text: size, and, since it is not swift enough to overtake the wild reindeer, it preys

35.text: entirely on the domesticated herds. In winter the wolf selects for its raids

36.text: dark, windy nights, or those with heavy snowfalls. Oftentimes several wolves

37.text: make a joint attack from various points. In such case they may in a single,

38.text: night kill several scores of reindeer, and — what is worse — disperse the

39.text: herd so widely that some of the younger animals cannot be found again.

40.text: The Chukchee consider the wolf a shaman, who, among other things, possesses

41.text: a charmed hood of thick hare-skin as white as snow. To make his raid suc-

42.text: cessful, he will put it over the herdsman’s head when snow is falling, and
